title: How Can a Jellyfish Sting in a Millionth of a Second?
description:
What actually happens when a jellyfish stings you? See how stinging cells fire a coiled harpoon without a brain, why the first part of the shot lasts just 700 nanoseconds in hydra, and why a dead jellyfish on the beach can still sting.

topic: What actually happens when a jellyfish stings you?
script: A jellyfish can sting you, in under a millionth of a second, without a brain, and you'd never see it coming. So what actually happens, when one of them stings you? First, meet the animal. Jellyfish have been drifting through the ocean, for more than 500 million years. And they've never had a brain. They also have no heart, no bones, and no blood. What they have instead, is a simple net of nerves, spread through a soft, see-through body. So when a jellyfish stings you, it isn't angry. It isn't even really aware of you. Most of them just drift, and let their tentacles do the work. Now zoom in on one tentacle. It's covered in thousands of tiny stinging cells. And inside each cell sits a capsule, called a nematocyst. Several of them could fit, across a single human hair. Packed inside that capsule, is a long, hollow thread, coiled up like a spring, with a sharp tip waiting at the front. Think of it as a loaded harpoon, sitting in a bath of venom. The pressure in there is huge, about 150 times normal air pressure. That's dozens of times stronger, than the air in a car tire. So what sets it off? Each cell has a tiny trigger on the outside. Bump it, or hit it with the right chemicals, and the lid pops open. Seawater rushes in, the pressure takes over, and the harpoon fires. No brain tells it to. The cell mostly acts on its own. Now here's the part that's hard to believe. In 2006, scientists filmed this, in hydra, a tiny relative of the jellyfish. Their camera shot over a million frames per second. And the first part of the shot, was over in just 700 nanoseconds. That's seven ten-millionths of a second. The tip hit up to five million g's. people tend to black out at around six. And a mantis shrimp's famous punch, reaches about ten thousand. Because that tip is so tiny, the pressure where it lands, is in the range of a bullet. It's strong enough to pierce a crab's shell. So what happens in your skin? After the tip punches in, the thread turns itself inside out, and the capsule squeezes venom through it. Some of those toxins punch holes in cells. Others go after nerves. One cell alone does almost nothing. But brushing a tentacle sets off thousands, all at once, and that's the sudden burn you feel. For most people, it's more painful than dangerous, though a few species, like some box jellyfish, are seriously dangerous. And since nothing here needs a brain, things get strange. A dead jellyfish on the beach, can still sting you. Clownfish live among stinging anemones, the jellyfish's cousins, because their slime lacks a chemical, that helps set those cells off. And some sea slugs eat stinging cells, without firing them, then store them in their own bodies, and use them on their own enemies. So that sting wasn't an attack. It was thousands of tiny machines, each doing the one thing it was built for, half a billion years in the making. Next up, why can you hold a crocodile's jaws shut, with your bare hands?
key_facts: Hydra nematocyst discharge as short as 700 nanoseconds, up to 5.41 million g (Nüchter et al. 2006, 15 MPa capsule pressure, >7 GPa at impact)
Jellyfish fossils over 500 million years old; no brain, heart, bones or blood
Nematocysts 5-15 microns; can still fire after a jellyfish dies
Clownfish mucus nearly lacks sialic acid, an anemone sting trigger
Aeolid sea slugs store unfired nematocysts and use them against predators
